extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners examining computer-implemented business method patent applications
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for formulating, supporting, and communicating rejections under 35 U.S.C. 103 (obviousness) for applications directed to computer-implemented business method inventions, including how to gather facts, evaluate obviousness, consider rebuttal evidence, and write Office actions. Focused on examiner procedures and legal standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graham Inquiry: determine scope and content of the prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Determining the scope and content of the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The content of the prior art is determined at the time the invention was made to avoid hindsight. The examiner determines the most probable field of search for the invention as claimed and described in the specification. The most probable field of search includes the same field of applicant's endeavor as well as analogous areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graham Inquiry: ascertain differences between prior art and claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Ascertaining the differences between the prior art and the claims in issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ascertaining differences requires interpreting the claim language and considering both the claimed invention and the prior art reference as a whole. Examiner should identify which piece of art is closest, what differences exist with the closest prior art, and where the individual differences are shown in the prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graham Inquiry: resolve level of ordinary skill in the art
rubrics_metrics.description: Resolving the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors to consider include: the educational level of the inventor; type of problems encountered in the art; prior art solutions; rapidity with which innovations are made; sophistication of the technology; educational level of active workers in the field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graham Inquiry: evaluate objective evidence (secondary considerations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluating any objective evidence of nonobviousness (i.e., so-called 'secondary considerations').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of objective evidence include commercial success; long-felt need; failure of others to solve the problem; skepticism of experts; copying. Such evidence must be commensurate in scope with the claims and there must be a nexus between the evidence and claimed features. Mere arguments are not evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine what to search for (claim scope and breadth of search)
rubrics_metrics.description: The scope of the claimed invention must be clearly determined prior to searching.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: During examination, claims are given the broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification. The search should not be limited to literal claim elements and should, insofar as possible, cover subject matter the examiner reasonably anticipates might be incorporated into applicant's amendment. The initial search should be sufficiently complete such that only an update search is needed in the second action, unless amendments require further searching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine where to search (field of search selection and prioritization)
rubrics_metrics.description: When determining where to search and what to search for, the examiner must consider the invention 'as a whole.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan a thorough search by (1) identifying the field of search; (2) selecting proper tools; and (3) determining an appropriate search strategy. Consider domestic patents, foreign patent documents, and nonpatent literature (NPL). Do not eliminate any source unless there is reasonable certainty no more pertinent references will be found there. Prioritize search areas starting with the same field of endeavor, then analogous arts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select appropriate search tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Choice of search tools is a key factor in ensuring the most relevant prior art is found.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners are provided both manual and automated tools; choose based on knowledge of coverage, strengths and weaknesses. In fast-moving/high-tech arts where patent literature may lag, take special care to include NPL and use tools specialized for NPL coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop search strategy for each tool
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine the appropriate search strategy for each search tool selected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appropriate search strategy should be determined case-by-case and may involve consultation with other examiners and supervisory patent examiners where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine whether found art qualifies as prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102
rubrics_metrics.description: Art found during the search must qualify as 'prior art' as defined by 35 U.S.C. 102 before it can be used to reject a claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider when the art became public, who was the source (inventor or another party), and whether the art satisfies the enablement provision of 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph. Subject matter that is prior art under 102 can support a 103 rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documentary prior art (printed publications and electronic publications)
rubrics_metrics.description: Publicly available documents, such as issued patents and printed publications, are commonly used in prior art rejections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A reference is a 'printed publication' if accessible to the public. Electronic publications, including online databases or Internet publications, are considered 'printed publications' provided the publication was accessible to persons concerned with the art to which the document relates. Printed documents usually have publication dates facilitating objective determination of prior art status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-documentary prior art (admissions and common knowledge)
rubrics_metrics.description: Publicly available information in non-published form may qualify as prior art (e.g., admissions, well-known scientific principles, common knowledge).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Admissions: statements in the specification or other prosecution papers that certain information was known prior to the date of invention constitute prior art and can be used for 103 rejections without corroborating reference. Common/prior knowledge: examiner may take official notice of facts 'well known in the art' but this practice should be applied sparingly; if based on personal knowledge, data should be stated specifically and supported by an affidavit if called for. If applicant does not seasonably traverse a well-known statement, it may be taken as admitted prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine relevancy and closeness of prior art to the claimed subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate which art is closest, whether the prior art shows all differences not shown by the closest prior art, and whether the art suggests combining individual teachings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continuously evaluate art found during the search to identify the closest reference and map claim differences to specific portions of prior references; determine where individual differences are shown in the art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prima facie obviousness — required factual/legal foundations
rubrics_metrics.description: To establish a prima facie case of obviousness, three basic criteria must be met: (1) some suggestion or motivation to modify or combine references; (2) a reasonable expectation of success; and (3) the prior art must teach or suggest all claim limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The initial burden is on the examiner to provide some suggestion of the desirability of doing what the applicant has done. Both the suggestion to combine and the reasonable expectation of success must be founded in the prior art and not in applicant's disclosure. The rationale for combining may be in the references themselves or presented as a convincing line of reasoning grounded in the prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale may be derived from sources other than direct reference disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: The rationale for a rejection may be reasoned from common knowledge in the art, official notice, a known business principle, art-recognized equivalents, or legal precedent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A simple statement that a difference is a 'design choice' or 'lacks an advantage or unexpected result' is insufficient—these are conclusions, not factual rationale. Reliance on legal precedent is appropriate only when a common factual basis is established. If applicant has demonstrated criticality of a limitation, it is not appropriate to rely solely on case law to support obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of hindsight and improper motivation
rubrics_metrics.description: Impermissible hindsight and application of per se rules must be avoided; do not rely on applicant's disclosure as the motivation to combine references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examiner must step backward in time into the shoes of the hypothetical person of ordinary skill and determine whether the claimed invention 'as a whole' would have been obvious. The tendency to resort to hindsight is often difficult to avoid but must be guarded against. Proposed motivations must be specific and directed to the claim differences, not general or hindsight-driven.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner burden and required specificity in Office action
rubrics_metrics.description: When rejecting a claim, administrative due process and 35 U.S.C. 132 require that applicant be adequately notified of the reasons for the rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office action should designate the particular part of a reference being relied upon (37 CFR § 1.104(c)(2)); articulate the differences between the claim and the closest prior art; state where differences are found or suggested; explain how the teachings are combined; and explain why the combination would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill at the time of the invention. Do not cite applicant's disclosure as the motivation. After applicant rebuttal, reconsider the initial determination in view of the entire record before imposing any rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rebuttal evidence standards and types
rubrics_metrics.description: Once a prima facie case is established, the burden shifts to the applicant to present evidence rebutting obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence types: (1) evidence of unexpected or nonobvious properties/advantages (comparative examples, affidavits/declarations under 37 CFR 1.132), and (2) evidence of real world activities (commercial success, long-felt need, failure of others, skepticism, copying). Arguments are not evidence. Comparative tests must compare the claimed invention to the closest prior art, be commensurate in scope, not conducted under special conditions, and show truly significant differences. A nexus must be established between the objective evidence and the claimed features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of official notice and examiner personal knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiner may take official notice of facts 'well known in the art' but this should be applied sparingly and be supported when challenged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a rejection is based on facts within the examiner's personal knowledge, data should be stated as specifically as possible and, when called for by the applicant, supported by an affidavit from the examiner. Such an affidavit is subject to contradiction and explanation by applicant affidavits or other evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibited/insufficient rationales and common improper rejection patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain forms of rationale are improper: general motivation statements, motivations contrary to the stated purpose of the reference, motivations not directed to the claim differences, and hindsight-driven combinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in the guidance illustrate improper rejections: using an overly general motivation like 'improve efficiency' that could cover many alterations; proposing a motivation that would contradict the reference's purpose; proposing motivations not addressing the claim differences. Such rejections are improper and must be avoided.
